extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent litigators, judges, and law students interested in patent litigation doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal and normative analysis of how questions of patent validity should be categorized (law, fact, or mixed question) and the procedural consequences for litigation, appellate review, and judicial review of Patent Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (§102, §103, §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents must satisfy statutory requirements including novelty, nonobviousness, and adequate description/enabling disclosure — phrased on the page as inventions must be “novel, nonobvious, and clearly and fully described.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are foundational substantive standards: novelty (35 U.S.C. §102), nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103), and written description/enablement/utility (35 U.S.C. §112). The Article uses these statutory requirements as the core legal yardsticks against which validity is assessed and as examples throughout the law-versus-fact discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter (§101) / judge-made exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether an invention falls within statutory categories of patent-eligible subject matter and whether it is excluded by judge-made exceptions (e.g., abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article discusses eligibility primarily via Supreme Court doctrine (Alice/Mayo) and treats eligibility as an example of an area where the Federal Circuit sometimes treats the issue as predominantly legal; it highlights that eligibility analysis often looks like judge-made doctrine best understood through case-specific examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a single prior-art reference discloses every element of a claimed invention (anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article treats anticipation as a largely fact-driven inquiry (see Section III.B.1) involving case-specific factual determinations such as the content of prior art and its public availability; this supports treating anticipation questions as fact-intensive/mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description (and enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent specification discloses the invention sufficiently to show possession (written description) and whether it enables a person of ordinary skill to make and use the invention (enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in Section III.B (compare enablement), these doctrines require factual inquiries about what the specification teaches and what a person of ordinary skill would be able to do, supporting their characterization as fact- or mixed-question issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed invention has a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed alongside other §112-related inquiries (Section III.B.3); treated as case-specific and thus fact-laden in the Article's survey of validity doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (Graham framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 using Graham factors: scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonobviousness is discussed as paradigmatic of mixed/law-based-on-facts issues: underlying Graham inquiries are factual (prior art, level of skill, motivation to combine, expectation of success, secondary considerations) while the ultimate legal determination of obviousness has been variously characterized; the Article argues it should be treated as a mixed question and typically reviewed deferentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law vs fact vs mixed-question classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a particular validity issue is a pure question of law, a question of fact, or a mixed question requiring application of law to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification has substantial procedural consequences (who decides, stage of resolution, standard of proof, standard of appellate review). The Article emphasizes that the Supreme Court describes ultimate patent validity as a question of law based on underlying facts, but argues for treating validity as a mixed question closer to the factual end of the spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review (de novo vs deferential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which standard (de novo, clear-error, substantial-evidence, or a mixed standard) an appellate court applies to validity determinations depending on whether the question is legal, factual, or mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing U.S. Bank, the Article explains that the standard for mixed questions depends on whether the question entails primarily legal or factual work: de novo if it develops auxiliary legal principles; deferential if it requires marshaling and weighing case-specific evidence and credibility judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides validity (judge vs jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the judge or the jury should decide patent validity and under what circumstances (bench trial, jury trial, bifurcation, special verdicts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article documents current practice where juries sometimes decide validity (often via general verdicts) despite validity being labeled a legal question; it argues that treating validity as a fact-heavy mixed question would generally favor judge decisions (reasoned opinions) and appropriate deference on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof / Presumption of validity (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An issued patent is presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. §282; patent challengers must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence (Microsoft v. i4i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article highlights the tension of applying an evidentiary standard to a purportedly legal question and argues that viewing validity as mixed resolves that tension by permitting application of a heightened standard to the overall mixed determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the presumption of validity to factual/legal aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the presumption of validity and its heightened standard of proof apply to subsidiary factual findings only, to legal aspects, or to the ultimate mixed question of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article recommends applying the presumption to the overall mixed-question determination to avoid awkward line-drawing between factual and legal components and to clarify analysis (e.g., wrap subsidiary questions like motivation to combine into the ultimate §103 determination under the heightened standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/stage for resolving validity (motion to dismiss, summary judgment, bench trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: At what procedural stage validity may be resolved — pleading stage, summary judgment, bench trial, or jury trial — and how the law-fact classification affects that timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-laden/mixed issues generally cannot be resolved at early stages without a developed record; treating validity as mixed gives district courts flexibility to pick posture (e.g., bench trial, bifurcation) better suited to case-specific determinations and avoids premature disposals on thin records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of jury findings (general vs special verdicts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether juries should return general verdicts (winner-loser) or special verdicts/findings on specific factual issues submitted by the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes that general verdicts are common but odd for legal questions and can produce doctrinal paradoxes; special verdicts or detailed interrogatories reduce ambiguity by surfacing factual findings that a judge can apply to legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting claim scope (claim construction) as a procedural and substantive step that affects both infringement and validity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markman teaches that claim construction is for the judge; the Article suggests using claim construction to reduce jury trials and to permit judges to decide patentability more effectively, thereby streamlining litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/institutional inquiry for assigning decisionmaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which institution (trial judge, jury, or appellate court) is better situated to resolve a given mixed question by a pragmatic, functional analysis of institutional competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article urges moving beyond reflexive legal/factual labels toward a functional inquiry (who is better situated), as U.S. Bank suggests, to decide whether deference or de novo review and whether judge or jury adjudication is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of factuality in underlying inquiries (level of ordinary skill, prior art content, expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many subsidiary validity issues (e.g., level of ordinary skill in the art, scope and content of prior art, motivation to combine, expectation of success, what prior art discloses) are case-specific factual matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these subsidiary inquiries are fact-intensive and require weighing evidence and credibility, they support treating ultimate validity as a mixed question entitled to deferential appellate review when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of Patent Office actions and administrative-law conceptualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether judicial review of the Patent Office should be treated like ordinary administrative review (with deference) and whether litigation over validity is effectively judicial review of agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues that viewing validity as a mixed question would bring judicial review of PTO actions into the mainstream of administrative law, justify appropriate deference, and favor reasoned bench decisions over jury verdicts when resolving agency-like questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative rule proposed: treat patent validity as a mixed question
rubrics_metrics.description: The Article's central normative thesis: all questions of patent validity should be considered mixed questions of law and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating validity as mixed would simplify doctrine, allow judges to issue reasoned opinions on the record, increase appropriate appellate deference, clarify the presumption of validity's application, and permit more pragmatic procedural choices (e.g., deciding validity by judge with deferential review) to improve efficiency and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of classification for appeals and litigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: How labeling validity as law, fact, or mixed affects incentives: stage of resolution, cost of litigation, likelihood of jury trial, appeals behavior, and potential for prolonged litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article explains that characterizing validity as mixed and reviewing deferentially would reduce incentives to prolong cases seeking appellate reversal, lower costs by reducing jury trials and repeated proceedings, and better align review standards with the case-specific nature of patentability determinations.
